Welcome to live coverage of Sunday afternoon’s 2pm Premier League kick-offs. Enzo Maresca faces the unenviable task of following Pep Guardiola’s decade of dominance at Manchester City and his reign begins in earnest with a visit from Bournemouth, who themselves are ushering in a new era after Marco Rose succeeded Andoni Iraola. A bruising 3-0 defeat in the Community Shield last weekend does not bode well for City’s hopes of closing the gap to Arsenal, but Maresca will be telling his charges that this afternoon is a fresh start: a new week and a new competition, plus Erling Haaland has a new haircut…

The Italian’s squad has been shorn of World Cup winner Rodri, who departed for Barcelona this week, and the spotlight will turn to £116m club-record signing Elliot Anderson who is expected to make his Premier League debut with City. Jérémy Doku is out for two to three weeks after suffering a calf injury, which could open the door for Jack Grealish, with City bereft of wide options. City will have their work cut out as Bournemouth, fresh off a historic sixth-place finish last season, look to extend their 18-match unbeaten run from the end of last season. The Cherries won three of their five pre-season matches, which included an eye-catching 10-1 victory over Serie A side Genoa.

Brighton and Hove Albion welcome Aston Villa to the Amex for their 2026-27 season opener having travelled 220 miles north of the Arctic Circle to play Norwegian side Tromso in their Europa Conference league play-off on Thursday. Fabian Hurzeler’s side face the defending Europa League champions without Carlos Baleba, who is on the brink of joining Manchester United, as well as injured wingers Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh. While Unai Emery has lost key players in Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Ezri Konsa and Lucas Digne, the funds raised has gone towards seven signings, with Zion Suzuki, the Japan goalkeeper, in line to make his first start for Villa.

#2168. 'Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It's my first time in Old Trafford!' - An afternoon with my 10-year-old inside the Theatre of Screams for Carrick's last stand

Published: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026

‘Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’ he asks earnestly, handing me a leaflet that announces: ‘Enough is Enough! Empty Old Trafford! Leave the stadium in the 21st minute. 21 years of failed ownership. Glazers OUT! Ineos OUT!’

More than 70,000 spectators leaving their seat and walking out of the stadium in the 21st minute have been quite the statement, especially live on Sky Sports.

But as admirable as Saeed TV’s aim is (I discover later he is some sort of youtuber), it’s hard to see gain any traction.

‘Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It’s my first time in Old Trafford,’ I am told as we continue to meander up Matt Busby Way, a declaration from my 10-year-old that causes a fair bit of mirth among the crowd.

Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’

‘What’s wrong with the owners anyway?’ Dan enquires innocently, which leads to a bind.

How deep down the rabbit-hole should I go with my ten-year-old on his first visit to the Theatre of Dreams.

It’s probably not the time or place to try and explain leveraged buyouts and how much debt the Glazers have saddled the club with, £1.2 billion at the last count while taking millions out of it in dividends. Do I need to go further back and talk about Rock of Gibraltar’s unexpected success on the track and the concept of stud fees?

‘They are not putting enough money into the team and taking loads of money out of the club,’ is all I offer.

‘When Manchester City need a midfielder, they can buy Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez while United have to make do with someone who was sitting on Chelsea’s bench.’

He doesn’t look convinced that’s much of a reason to walk out of a football but as the cathedral of consumerism that is the Manchester United megastore has appeared, he forgets about United’s disastrous ownership model – for now, at least.

During his doomed attempt to coax Jurgen Klopp to Old Trafford around 2014, Ed Woodward apparently told him that United was the sporting version of Disneyland.

And to be sardined inside the megastore in the couple of hours before kick-off, you have to accept that the much-maligned former CEO may have been right about one thing.

Think Arnott’s a couple of days before Christmas, just with a lot more people. You even need to pass through airport-like security before even entering and spend your dosh.

One of the common refrains among United supporters is why are the Glazers holding onto the club when they don’t even seem to care.

Thirty seconds inside the megastore on match-day and you realise why the Americans are so keen to hold onto the asset they’re bleeding dry – and they probably care a great deal.

Dan gets obligatory photo at statue of United's holy trinity, a moment he will look back on

Even with the team languishing in the relegation zone, having won a single league game all season, people are keen to spend, spend, spend.

I see people wandering around with five or six different shirts, from different eras (I did succumb and bought Dan the black shirt from 95-96 season, because it reminds me of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and better times!)

You can get a photo with a replica of a Premier League trophy. That’s just £10. Or Lego sets of Old Trafford or the Munich clock.

That will just set you back £25.  For many in this shop, it seems allowing the club to empty their wallet is as much a part of the day as the actual football.

There are other parts of the ritual, which remain and have yet to be infected by the poisonous atmosphere around the club – and remind the three dads bringing their kids to Old Trafford for the first time of better days.

Such as curry chips and battered sausage from Lou Macari’s chipper. And the customary photo in front of the statue of the holy trinity of Best, Law and Charlton.

The megastore was the one place that seemed immune to the toxicity in the air. Once outside again and all that could be heard was the moans and groans, mainly because Shea Lacey wasn’t starting.

Coming here since the 1990s, we have seen the skyline of Manchester transformed as it became a sleek, modern city. It seems the one place that hasn’t changed is Old Trafford. It has remained the same.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium – and not just because of the leaking roof. It could do with a lick or two of paint.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium

No wonder Big Sir Jim is determined to plough ahead with his plans to make a crudely-designed circus tent ‘the Wembley of the North.’ Not that there is anyone inside Old Trafford of the same mind.

Senne Lammens has just trotted onto the field with Tom Heaton and Karl Darlow to do their pre-match warm-up when the chants start, telling Jim Ratcliffe he can stick his new stadium up his posterior.

It is a weird atmosphere, with all the chanting against the owners – both Glazers and Ineos – and nothing being sung in support of the players.

As my friend points out it must be so difficult for the team to show the best of themselves when things are this toxic in the stadium.

Dan has been to the Jodi Stand enough times on a Friday night to know there is plenty of choice and crude language at football matches, but still I nearly felt at covering his ears at some of the stuff being sung in Old Trafford last Sunday, especially that directed at CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

We had hoped that things might have been different when the game kicked off, but within a minute, Aston Villa had scored.

And three minutes later, they had scored again when Lammens fumbled Alysson’s shot into Nicolas Jackson’s path. Maybe walking out in the 21st minute wasn’t such a bad idea.

The crowd’s ire had gone from the owners to the players now, with a sustained chant of ‘You are not fit to wear the shirt.’ United did rally and by half-time, it was 2-2. But the mood was still dismal as we queued for a quick beer.

The 1958 Group had asked fans not to buy booze, another protest against the owners. But it seemed nobody was paying much attention to that.

One of the issues at United is that there seem to be too many splintered fan groups – there is also ClaimBackUnited and Fan Coalition ’58 – as well as Saeed TV, who seemed to be on his own solo run.

We didn’t feel bad about ignoring the booze ban, as everyone was doing it. And within a couple of minutes of the second-half, we saw the reason why. You need to fortify yourself to watch Diogo Dalot try to defend.

For much of the second-half, it seemed like Michael Carrick’s brief tenure was going to peter out in a forgettable defeat, as Villa seemed to manage the game perfectly.

Dan and his friends were growing frustrated, pointing out the players weren’t doing what their coaches tell them to do on a weekly basis, leading me to conclude that maybe my son’s under-11 side are better-coached than United.

The last on-pitch act of Carrick's tenure

And then there was the chaotic and crazy final few minutes in stoppage-time. And a draw that came out of nowhere and was celebrated like a victory.

That was the thing. Even though the mood inside the stadium was toxic for most of the game, even though the team were two down inside four minutes and the season has been a disaster, everyone still came away from Old Trafford, happy and with a smile on their face.

Only football can do that. More than that, perhaps only Manchester United – despite everything – can do that.

#2167. England's Euro 2028 mission starts NOW! Thomas Tuchel's men must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - or risk their 'DNA' cursing them yet again, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 16:10 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 14 November 2026

It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.

That is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for. The manner of his side’s capitulation - and the substitutions he made - in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium last July enraged the nation, but Tuchel said the fault was in the damned DNA of the English, that we were underlings, and that our players found it constitutionally impossible to keep hold of the ball.

Whatever Tuchel thinks, the fact remains that the tie against Lamine Yamal, Fabian Ruiz, Pedri and Mikel Oyarzabal and the rest of the world champions at the home of Atletico Madrid offers Tuchel and his players the opportunity to encourage themselves and their fans that they are not destined to be also-rans wired to fall at the final hurdle for evermore.

Spain are formidable opposition. They are on a record-breaking run of 43 matches unbeaten and have won their last 12 in succession. They haven't drawn a game since their June 15 game against Cape Verde in the World Cup. Their last defeat was on March 22, 2024, when they lost 1-0 to Colombia in a friendly. Some ask whether they are the best international side the world has ever seen.

‘Spain seem unbeatable,’ Tuchel said, when he walked into the press room at the Metropolitano on Saturday night and heard hymns of praise being lavished upon the opponents he is about to face.

‘They have a very strong identity and a very strong mentality. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are up for the fight. We are up for a spectacular match. We can see how far we can push the limits with the world champions in Madrid. The group is full of self-belief and rightly so.’

England must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - even if they have flaws

Thomas Tuchel must show he can find a way around the limitations presented by the 'DNA' he has complained about

This may be the toughest game that Tuchel’s England side play until the European Championships in 2028, where the final will be contested at Wembley, and they will play all their games at home. They need to go into that tournament with the belief that they can beat the best when the pressure is at its highest.

Beating Spain away in the final game of the group phase of the Nations League is not quite the same as a critical match at a major tournament but it is as stiff a challenge as Tuchel is going to face until then. Beating Croatia 7-0 in front of gangs of schoolkids in Rijeka last month was hailed as the best England performance of the Tuchel era. Which says it all, really.

It was a great performance in a relatively meaningless match. Now it is time for him to show that he can marshal an England side to succeed against the very best, not fall apart when the prize is in sight. His protestations of powerlessness in the aftermath of the Argentina defeat were not a good look for a coach who was hired with the idea that his coaching prowess and his game management could get England over the line.

Has he learned anything from the manner of the Argentina defeat? ‘This game against Spain will be proof of concept at the highest level,’ he said, ‘but we are up for it. I think we have taken the next step after the World Cup. The best thing is to trust our process and trust ourselves. We need to be clear about how we want to impose ourselves and I think that is all visible.’

Now it is time for him to show that he can find a way past the limitations of England’s footballing DNA, find a way to compete with Spain and France when it really matters, and find a way to end the culture of near misses that has come to be England’s lot in the last decade of appearances in semi-finals and finals.

England have played six matches since that day of crushing disappointment in Atlanta and scored 22 goals. But in the only one of those matches that really mattered, they lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley in the opening tie of their Nations League campaign at the end of September, a game in which they were largely outclassed by Luis de la Fuente’s team.

Spain are what England have to aim for. Tuchel mentioned their example and their ability and their mindset straight after the semi-final loss to Argentina. ‘Ball possession plays a crucial role,’ he said at his post-match press conference in Atlanta. ‘It’s maybe not in our DNA like it is in our Spanish DNA or in our Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball.’

This may well be their toughest game until the final of the 2028 European Championships, if they get that far

The England coach said more recently that England need to go back to trusting a traditional style that emphasises direct, high-intensity physicality rather than trying to copy Spanish patience in ball-retention. England, though, were taught a lesson in sophistication by the Spanish in September.

And for all the attention lavished on Yamal, Spain’s defence is the best in the world. Rodri, the shield for that defence and also the world’s best in the role, is not fit for this game but even without him, Spain’s back-line inspires an awful lot more confidence than England’s.

‘They were the best in the World Cup at the back,’ Declan Rice, England’s central midfielder, said on Saturday. ‘Defence wins you titles. Everyone talks about their attacking talent but you look at their central defenders, their full backs and the way their midfielders contribute to the defence, too.’

That defence will have to stop England’s resurgent front line, led by Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who could be flanked by Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers and backed up by the supreme talent of Jude Bellingham just behind them.

Bellingham’s improving relationship with Tuchel, which cannot have been harmed by the inclusion of Bellingham’s brother, Jobe, in this squad, is another reason to hope that England still retain the capacity to improve after the World Cup. The elder Bellingham has become England’s most influential player.

England at their best would be one of the few teams capable of extending them. Rice said on Saturday that the game between the two sides was ‘massive’. England need to prove they can find a way to get closer to the world champions. To beat them, Rice said, would be a ‘massive statement’.

‘Playing against them is a great incentive to win. It will show where we are as a group. We are trying to attack teams full throttle and with players like Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers in our attack, it feels as if it is going to take off one night and maybe tomorrow night will be the night. We can beat Spain. For sure, we can.’

Tuchel needs to prove England can win, not just be noble contenders. They need to prove that their DNA need not be a curse.

#2166. Sheffield United are having the last laugh over £6m Burnley deal

Sheffield United endured a tricky start to the Championship campaign, but Chris Wilder’s side have fought their way up the table in recent weeks and are having the last laugh regarding one transfer saga.

Following the sales of Andre Brooks, Callum O’Hare, and Gustavo Hamer in the summer, Sheffield United appeared to be in a spot of bother, especially with parachute payments running out.

The Blades had no choice but to rely solely on loans and free transfers, bringing in the likes of Ben Brereton Diaz, Romelle Donovan, Jordan Ayew, and Matt Doherty to subdued fanfare.

With almost no money to spend, Chris Wilder’s side saw themselves priced out of numerous deals, including one that would have reunited a former fan favourite with Bramall Lane.

Sheffield United were interested in bringing Bosnian centre-back Anel Ahmedhodzic back to the club over the summer, after Feyenoord made it abundantly clear that they were looking to sell the 27-year-old.

Ahmedhodzic initially joined the Blades in the summer of 2022 from French outfit Bordeaux, and across the next three years, he would make 114 appearances across all competitions for the South Yorkshire outfit, including 31 in the Premier League.

After Sheffield United were defeated in the 2025 Championship play-off final by Sunderland, Ahmedhodzic, along with the likes of Vinicius Souza and Kieffer Moore, left the club the following summer, with the Bosnian heading to Rotterdam to link up with Feyenoord.

However, after just one year at De Kuip and 36 appearances across all competitions, the defender was made available for transfer this summer, but it quickly became apparent that the Blades could not afford him, as a division rival swooped in under their noses.

Football League World has asked AI to predict the 2027/28 EFL Championship table if Manchester United and Manchester City were in it

Following their relegation from the Premier League and departures of Maxime Esteve, Joe Worrall, and Axel Tuanzebe, Burnley were in the market for defensive reinforcements.

Then under Nicky Hayen, the Clarets completed deals for Max Alleyne, Igor Julio, and Ahmedhodzic, with the latter heading to Turf Moor in a deal worth around £6 million.

It was viewed as a real coup for Burnley at the time, with Ahmedhodzic having ample Championship experience under his belt and at a decent age, but so far, he has struggled to justify that fee.

Amid Burnley’s struggles, the Bosnian has not helped stop the rot spreading in Lancashire, with the Clarets sitting in the relegation zone after 15 league games with just one win, and, with just six league appearances, he has found himself on the bench and out of the squad entirely in recent weeks.

Certainly, this is not how he would’ve imagined his return to England going, as those at Bramall Lane must be laughing.

With Ahmedhodzic joining Burnley, this didn’t stop Sheffield United’s own pursuit of defensive reinforcements, as with a deal for Leicester City’s Harry Souttar looking too expensive, Wilder turned to the loan market.

Coventry City centre-back Liam Kitching, following the Sky Blues’ promotion to the top flight, found himself out of Frank Lampard’s plans at the CBS Arena, and Wilder moved quickly to secure a deal for the Irishman.

Following his late move to South Yorkshire, Kitching has been an almost ever-present in the Blades’ back line alongside Japhet Tanganga, with ten league appearances so far, and reminding everyone why he was a crucial cog in Coventry’s promotion to the Premier League.

Having not paid a penny for Kitching, Sheffield United and Wilder must be laughing now after Ahmedhodzic's struggles with Burnley, as an expensive transfer bullet may have been dodged.

Would you have liked to have seen Anel Ahmedhodzic return to Sheffield United in the summer, or are you happy with Liam Kitching? Share your thoughts below!

With Burnley and Ahmedhodzic struggling at the foot of the Championship table and Sheffield United within touching distance of the play-offs, Wilder will surely be pleased with the way things have panned out.

Of course, had the Bosnian returned to Bramall Lane, then things could have gone differently, and he could be a key part of the side in South Yorkshire now.

But avoiding a £6 million fee and signing someone some people will argue is better, the Blades have come out on the right end of this saga, much to Burnley’s dismay.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#2164. Celtic & Southampton must be feeling fresh Stoke City transfer regret

Stoke City headed into the international break level on points with Birmingham City and Middlesbrough at the top of the Championship table, as Mark Robins will be looking to ensure his side can maintain this form upon their return to action.

Indeed, only Birmingham’s and Middlesbrough’s superior goal difference keeps Stoke off the top of the Championship table right now as things stand, with the Potters enjoying another excellent start to the campaign.

It was around this time last year when Stoke suffered a calamitous dip in form, as Robins must be doing everything he can to avoid a similar fate this time around.

A strong summer window will give the former Coventry City boss the belief that this year is different, and when they do return to action after the international break, he will be looking to one player in particular for a sizeable impact.

This most recent summer transfer window was Robins’ second in charge at the bet365 Stadium, and he will certainly be pleased with the business his side was able to conduct.

Lewis Baker, Steven Nzonzi, Tatsuki Seko, and Sorba Thomas left through the exit door, as the likes of Luke Graham, Ethan Galbraith, Djibril Soumare, George Hirst, and Jack McGlynn headed in the opposite direction.

McGlynn, alongside compatriot Luca Bombino, arrived in the Potteries late in the window, but he wouldn’t quite be the final addition, as Stoke completed a deal worth around £5 million for Northern Ireland international Justin Devenny.

Devenny, 23, began his career in the lower reaches of Scotland, predominantly plying his trade with Airdrieonians before being spotted by Crystal Palace in the summer of 2023.

The versatile midfielder made 60 appearances across all competitions for the Eagles during his two-year stay in South London, helping the club lift the FA Cup, UEFA Europa Conference League, and Community Shield, and before his move to Stoke, had numerous other admirers as well.

#2162. Red card for football chiefs as they announce ex-Premier League referee is dead aged 78 - when he is still alive and kicking

Published: 13:01 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 20:45 EST, 14 November 2026

A former Premier League referee was mistakenly declared dead by football chiefs this week.

On Tuesday, the Football Association of Wales (FAW) announced Keith Cooper had died aged 78. But he is alive and well.

The news reached the ears of the Wembley Cup final referee when he went out to his local sports centre for a flu jab only to be told: 'You were dead.'

The Football Association of Wales posted a statement online and a tribute on social media to announce his death, but then withdrew it within an hour.

Mr Cooper, who is the father of former Nottingham Forest and Leicester boss Steve Cooper, told a Welsh sports website: 'I walked into the sports centre yesterday to have my jab and the fellow went, "You were dead!"

'Well, I'm not dead, I'm here and I'm OK!'

The blunder appears to have emerged after the Wiltshire FA announced the death of another referee called Keith Cooper, who the football chiefs in Wales believed was the other Keith Cooper.

The FAW statement said: 'Keith was a well-known figure who enjoyed an exceptional career at both domestic and international level and would later hold the position of FAW Referees' Officer following his retirement in 1996.

On Tuesday, the Football Association of Wales (FAW) announced Keith Cooper had died aged 78

Mark Beeney goalkeeper of Leeds United is Sent Off of by Referee Keith A Cooper for hand ball outside the area during the Premier League match between Manchester United and Leeds United at Old Trafford on April 17, 1996 in Manchester, England

Former professional football John Fashanu is pictured with referee Keith Cooper during a Wimbledon F.C. match

'Born and raised in Pontypridd, he is considered one of Wales' best match officials through his highly-regarded status in the game.

'In addition to his work with FAW, Keith was also a valued member of the Wiltshire FA Council who recognised his 'integrity, passion and commitment' in their tribute to his services to the game.

'Everyone at the FAW sends their condolences to his family and friends at this sad time.'

Mr Cooper oversaw the 1994 League Cup final between Aston Villa and Manchester United, won by Villa 3-1, and worked in radio punditry after hanging up his whistle.

The FAW has not issued an explanation over the posted tribute. His family has not yet commented on the error.

But the unfortunate mistake has not spared the FAW from ridicule by other football fans.

One said: 'We always said there was only one Keith Cooper - turns out there are two.'

Another said: 'Glad the whistle wasn't blown too early on Keith and much respect to the family of the other one.'

#2161. Newcastle and Liverpool serve up thrilling tribute to Kevin Keegan

It had to end that way, didn’t it? A last-minute goal, a sense of what might have been and a helter-skelter contest that will take days to decipher.

Newcastle versus Liverpool became the Premier League’s most dramatic fixture when Kevin Keegan was manager here and, on the afternoon they flocked to the “cathedral on the hill” to pay tribute to the late, great superstar, we were treated to a contest that was in keeping with his narrative.

Liverpool operating with the discipline of a basketball team undoubtedly helped, and we can examine those gaping chasms soon enough, but the poignancy of seeing Matthias Jaissle looking as bereft as Keegan at Anfield 30 years ago at the final whistle was impossible to ignore.

Really, the German’s first match in charge of Newcastle should have ended with three points. His team are a work in progress – rich in youthful exuberance though prone to lapses – but how they fought, ran and worked to give the locals the result they wanted.

They were almost at the finish line, seconds away from beating Liverpool here for the first time since December 2015, but then Lewis Hall ran into Victor Muñoz, sending the Spanish substitute sprawling, and Stuart Attwell pointed to the penalty spot. Dominik Szoboszlai inflicted maximum damage.

Dominik Szoboszlai equalises from the spot in the 99th minute! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/0Ag9WitqHt

“I have clear thoughts,” Jaissle said quietly, as he was asked to reflect on the day-wrecking decision. “I guess you call it a soft penalty here. If you give it, you need to give a lot during this match and a lot during the season. I don’t know if it that is good for football.”

Here was the third time in four seasons Liverpool had scored in injury time in front of the Leazes Stand, after Darwin Núñez (2023) and Rio Ngumoha (2025), and their eighth goal beyond the 90th minute in collisions with Newcastle is a Premier League record against the same opponents.

No wonder he was stunned. Jaissle had spent idle moments in the build-up thinking about what might happen if Newcastle scored an early goal and, much to his delight, fantasy became reality in the most thrilling fashion. On this emotional afternoon, it was fitting the hosts scored first.

One of Keegan’s great early wins as Newcastle manager was in November 1993, when his team blew away Liverpool in the snow and Andy Cole scored a first-half hat-trick. His first goal that day came after five minutes and, by happy coincidence, the clock stopped at that moment for Anthony Elanga, too.

How Liverpool went from having a chance of their own to conceding 20 seconds later is something Andoni Iraola will have to address quickly, but that is what happened: Ryan Gravenberch should have shot, instead he passed and Amar Dedic intervened, his interception finding Will Osula.

Off Osula galloped, Liverpool’s defenders looking leaden-footed as they gave pursuit, and he ushered Elanga into open space. Once he was in the clear, he was not for catching and his shot was perfectly placed beyond Alisson Becker.

An electric start! Anthony Elanga gives Newcastle the lead inside 5 minutes! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/8DYYFJ9i6F

As Elanga was mobbed, the recriminations started. Fingers pointed at each other, Iraola spun around in dismay. Liverpool were easy to play against last season – Iraola’s Bournemouth had scored two identical goals against them on the opening day 12 months ago – and old habits die hard.

“We should finish the play,” Iraola conceded. “We created a great chance. We are on the edge of the box and have a clear opening to shoot and we decide not to. We don’t finish it properly and then you have to give credit to Elanga, who wins the race.”

What could Liverpool offer in response? The answer before the interval was nothing, other than a shot from Florian Wirtz that was well saved by Lukas Hornicek. The first half was wretched and it was difficult to see what had changed from the final throes of Arne Slot.

This, to be clear, is no criticism of Iraola, more a spotlight on players who need to step up. They did that momentarily in the second period, when Cody Gakpo equalised. He was afforded too much time by Newcastle’s defence but, still, his finish from 20 yards was super, zipping beyond Hornicek.

Cody Gakpo with a fine finish to equalise for Liverpool! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/cfDQWbES2v

But parity was secured for less than two minutes before Newcastle scored a near-carbon-copy second goal, another counter-attack – this was one led by the outstanding Yoane Wissa – ending with substitute Joe Willock finding a corner of Alisson’s net. Again the inquests followed.

"Wow!"Joe Willock restores Newcastle's advantage almost instantly with an exceptional finish! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/8IKPUgqapK

“We had the numbers to defend it better,” Iraola said. “It’s not like they caught us by surprise, but we didn’t defend it properly. We should compete for the first ball and probably make a foul, be a little more aggressive as we had the numbers to defend it.

“You don’t want to concede transitions and we’d been preparing them in the week for transitions.”

Why they didn’t follow the plan that had been set is something that Iraola must address, but he will be relieved that the days spent this week are not dissecting a defeat, as Wissa should have wrapped up the contest, only for Alisson to make a brilliant save to thwart the Congolese striker.

Those missed chances should not have mattered but in the final throes, Hall misjudged the angle Muñoz attacked him from, he got his challenge wrong and, after a pause, Attwell pointed to the spot. Given the agony Liverpool have inflicted, the outcome was as clear as black and white.

“We scored at the end, so you have a better taste,” Iraola said. “Before the game, we wouldn’t have signed for this result. It’s a reward. It’s only a point, but at least it’s something that’s deserved.”

Plenty would contest his conclusion. Liverpool got away with it – and Iraola is about to find the hard work is only just beginning.

A really soft one, if you give that, they’ll be more in the future, I’m not a fan of that.

Their heads are a little down but we know we had many challenges, we’re in a huge transition phase at the moment.

Peter Beardsley, Tino Asprilla and Shaka Hislop among Keegan’s former players watching on.

That was the player Eddie Howe thought he was signing last summer. It was the player Newcastle supporters thought was going to offer a major upgrade in the right wing position.

If Elanga has a better season this time around it will be a huge boost to new manager Matthias Jaissle.

An electric start! Anthony Elanga gives Newcastle the lead inside 5 minutes! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/8DYYFJ9i6F

Lewis Hall wins a challenge at the edge of the box which receives a roar of approval from the crowd, but Liverpool quickly settle into a long spell of possession, with Gravenberch turning away from pressure, but neglecting to shoot.

That roar turns to vociferous boos as Alexander Isak takes the kick-off.

Alan Shearer was one of those fans holding up a white card:

Banners are being unfurled in the Gallowgate End. Alan Shearer and Stuart Pearce are in the stands, and Les Ferdinand is pitchside speaking on Sky.

As you know it’s a transition phase and a huge challenge. There will be some activity in the transfer market new week, hopefully, but we go for it, we are as ready as we can be. That’s something we want to show the fans, we want to go all in.

As soon as I saw him on the pitch, I was falling in love. He is a great guy with great potential.

I’m not worried. As a manager, a player or a squad, if it is against you you want to play this kind of games.

Difficult call, Jeremy has very good skills with the ball, without the ball they will be very demanding today, playing against Wissa and Osula.

Alexander Isak is going to be in for the sort of hostile afternoon unseen in English football for years.

Not since Michael Owen has a player left Newcastle and been so universally despised. Owen was accused of ducking out of a relegation battle to ensure he secured a lucrative free transfer move after an injury-ravaged spell in the North East.

If anything, Isak was even worse, He went on strike, refusing to play for the club again, despite having three years left on his contract, in order to force a move to Liverpool. It felt like the ultimate betrayal and crossed a line with Geordies. They will love you and worship players as good as Isak, but if you behave like the Sweden international did you become the ultimate villain.

Isak was a superb player in black and white stripes, arguably their best since the takeover by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund in 2021. He was top goalscorer two years running and was the focal point of Eddie Hower’s attack as they qualified for the Champions League twice and won the Carabao Cup.

He could have been a Geordie legend, but he left in such an ugly and acrimonious fashion. Isak forced Newcastle to buckle from their not for sale stance, rejecting a pay rise and a new contract, insisting he would never play for the club again even if they refused to sell him, that he will be tarnished forever.

It is sad in many ways and shows the ugly side of the game. I’m told he does regret the manner of his exit, especially his falling out with Howe. They have not spoken since. It has weighed heavily on him since his move to Anfield.

Sir Kenny Dalglish and Bobby Moncur are the representatives of both clubs with wreaths, and Shola Ameobi is behind Dalglish. Ian Rush is also in attendance, who spent one season on Tyneside in the twilight of his career when Dalglish was the manager.

There will be a powerful expression of unity between Newcastle United and Liverpool supporters in memory of their shared icon, Kevin Keegan, before this afternoon’s game.

A man who meant so much to both clubs: a phenomenal player for Liverpool and a force of nature who transformed Newcastle as both a player and a manager.

The cooperation between the two to ensure St James’ Park can deliver a special tribute to a remarkable figure in English football has been heartwarming.

The sale of Curtis Jones to Inter Milan means that for the first time since Liverpool came into existence in 1892, the prospect of them going through the season without fielding a player who was born in the city for a game is real. That will surely sting Liverpool fans more than most, given the city’s strong sense of regional identity. You can read more on the subject in this article by Dominic King. Trent on loan in January, anyone?

These are early days, but the energy and purpose he has brought to the job have impressed everyone at all levels of the club. Clear communication is at the heart of everything. He explains what he expects, what he needs and what has to be done, no matter who the conversation is with.

It is fitting that Newcastle United vs Liverpool is a Premier League opening weekend fixture following the death of Kevin Keegan at the age of 75 last month.

All corners of St James’ Park will pay tribute and show their appreciation for the former player and manager who means a great deal to both sets of supporters.

Fans will find a printed message from the Keegan family on the back of black and white cards on their seat, which they will hold up to display a mural before kick-off.

As well as playing for both clubs, Keegan was Newcastle’s manager when they were beaten by a last-gasp Stan Collymore goal at Anfield in April 1996, a 4-3 defeat remembered as one of the great Premier League games.

This fixture usually delivers entertainment, and with new managers Matthias Jaissle and Andoni Iraola promising front-footed, ‘vertical’ football, there should be goals. That was certainly the case last August, when Newcastle fought back from two down with 10 men, before Rio Ngumoha scored a memorable winner.

It has been a summer of tumult for Newcastle, losing manager Eddie Howe, as well as key players Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes. There has been bullish talk of “Newcastle 2.0” from David Hopkinson, the club’s chief executive, and the club believe they have found a promising coach, but fans have understandably revised expectations downwards.

Liverpool are a difficult team to read; champions only 18 months ago but brittle last season, which resulted in Arne Slot’s dismissal. Iraola’s appointment is a shift back towards Jurgen Klopp’s style. That will be music to the ears of Anfield regulars, but holes remain in the squad. Central midfield has not been replenished; they need a Mohamed Salah replacement, and their strength at full-back is questionable. #2160. Roberto Di Matteo lifts lid on West Brom decision that shocked him

Roberto Di Matteo has admitted that he was ‘shocked’ West Brom sacked him back in 2011 as they battled to stay in the Premier League.

The Italian had a successful playing career, and he turned to management after retiring, initially starting out with MK Dons.

A move to Albion would follow, and Di Matteo would also work for Chelsea, Schalke and Aston Villa, with the high point undoubtedly coming with the Blues, who he won the Champions League and FA Cup with as interim boss.

Whilst nothing will surpass winning those trophies with Chelsea, Di Matteo really made his name as a manager during his time at The Hawthorns with West Brom.

After making the step up from League One outfit MK Dons, Di Matteo built an Albion side that won promotion to the Premier League in his first season at the club.

They did so by playing a brand of football that the fans really enjoyed, and they carried that into the top flight. Whilst an opening day 6-0 defeat at Chelsea was concerning, the players quickly adapted to the Premier League.

The Baggies had picked up 15 points from their first nine games, which included a memorable 3-2 win at Arsenal, a 2-2 draw at Old Trafford, and they also picked up a point from Tottenham.

So, Albion were performing very well, and they continued the entertaining style of play that had made them such a good watch the season before.

However, that form didn’t continue, and Di Matteo was ultimately dismissed in February, after a miserable period of seven defeats in nine.

And, speaking to Mick McCarthy and Tony Pulis on The Managers podcast, Di Matteo couldn’t hide how disappointed he was at the decision, with Albion outside the relegation zone at the time.

“I was a bit surprised and shocked. We’ve all worked in smaller clubs, so when you have injuries to one or two key players, it’s difficult. Up until the Christmas period we were looking really good, but Jonas Olsson, the centre-back, got injured for a while, and one or two others were not available.

“In the Christmas period, you play every two or three days and you don’t have a deep squad, so you struggle a bit. But, again, we were coming out of it, and I was really shocked.”

You can understand why Di Matteo was surprised at the decision, as he will have been tasked with keeping the team in the league, and he will argue he was on track to do that.

They had been on a terrible run over a period of a few months, and they would say the trend was pointing towards relegation.

Birmingham City's 2026/27 season has got off to a remarkable start on the pitch, with supporters starting to dream about what might be possible under Chris Davies.

The 41-year-old previously split opinion amongst Blues fans, especially after the way in which the 2025/26 Championship season panned out following continued investment from Knighthead Capital Management.

The club's American investors have vowed to change plenty in such a short space of time, and that doesn't just concern the outlook of Davies' squad in the near future as they chase a Premier League return, but the city of Birmingham as a whole.

Tom Wagner has been heralded for the work he has already put in and what he is planning towards as Blues look to finally realise their potential.

The idea of looking at the past to move forward can often be frowned upon, but for Wagner and Co. doing exactly that means that Birmingham fans are never likely to lose sight of their identity as the club embarks on a new era.

Last season may have been one of mixed fortunes for Birmingham and their supporters on the pitch, but that didn't mean it wasn't historic in other ways.

Indeed, just days before Blues celebrated their 150th anniversary game with a 4-1 rout over Norwich City, the club unveiled the design and name of its upcoming 62,500-seater stadium, which will stand tall less than a mile away from St. Andrew's @ Knighthead Park.

Blues recently confirmed a major decision relating to the building of the Sports Quarter

The Powerhouse will pay tribute to the Second City's rich industrial heritage, embodied by its name and design, and that comes across in more ways than one.

The Powerhouse will be the centrepiece of a multi-billion Sports Quarter project that will transform the Bordesley Green area with multiple commercial and retail hubs adjacent to the stadium.

Whilst the chimney-themed design has received major criticism from rival fanbases and beyond, those associated with the club will love how it will repurpose some of Birmingham's rich history.

Over 1,000 bricks which helped structure the City Hospital in Winson Green - built in 1912 as Birmingham Workhouse Infirmary - are being repurposed for the Powerhouse to stand tall on the former site of the Adderley Park Brickworks.

Blues fans, how excited are you to move into the Powerhouse? Comment below!

City Hospital has been closed since 2024, with the former site making way for a 750-home development adjacent to the Birmingham and Wolverhampton Main Line Canal, approximately 4.1 miles away from St. Andrew's.

"Lovingly salvaged, cleaned, sorted and restored by local experts, the original bricks from Adderley Park Brickworks will be incorporated into the Powerhouse – Birmingham City's future home and a defining part of the city’s Sports Quarter," a section of a statement on Blues' website confirming the purchase of said bricks read.

In recent months, more work has gone into how the overall Sports Quarter and the Powerhouse stadium will look ahead of a planned opening in the summer of 2031.

Many Blues fans are excited by what is to come, as emotional as it will be when the club have to leave St. Andrew's, having called their current stadium home since the year 1906.

In May, mutiple 'CGI' images were generated and shared by Birmingham's official social media accounts, including how various hospitality packages will be incorporated into the chimney designs.

This includes a high-level view of the pitch which will be named the 'Chimney Seats', as well as 'Restaurant with a View', which will allow guests a view of the city's main skyline, which stands approximately two miles away.

As previously mentioned, Knighthead have certainly done their utmost to embrace themselves in various cultural aspects associated with the West Midlands.

The Sports Quarter will provide thousands of jobs for locals, whilst also increasing the economy. In the meantime, the investment firm has also acquired stakes in Birmingham Phoenix alongside former Blues academy graduate and Real Madrid star, Jude Bellingham.

The effort which has gone into such a transformative project has not been underestimated by Blues fans, and it has been particularly evident how they feel about Wagner in his recent returns to St. Andrew's after unfortunately suffering a stroke in January.

#2157. Family's fury as 'elite' athlete twin brothers are arrested by ICE while on their way to college in Alabama

Published: 20:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 21:42 EST, 14 November 2026

A dismayed mother and father spoke out after their 'elite' athlete twin sons were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as they returned to their Alabama college.

Wallace State Community College soccer players Luis and Carlos Orta Santoro, 19, were taken into ICE custody after a traffic stop on November 4 while on their way to campus, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported.

The Venezuelan twins were returning from visiting their parents, Carlos Enrique Orta and Reyna Santoro de Orta, in Georgia when they were arrested by a Lincoln Police Department officer during a traffic stop in east-central Alabama.

The brothers graduated from Lawrenceville's Archer High School after a successful varsity soccer career that included a first ever region title for the school.

'This is the house of two elite soccer players,' Carlos Enrique Orta, their father, told the outlet.

Luis and Carlos are asylum seekers who applied for protections after legally entering the US on a tourist visa, like their parents.

That visa expired and the twins were granted US work permits and Georgia driver's licenses, according to the outlet.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, told the Daily Mail on Saturday that the brothers had legally entered the US with permission to stay on a temporary basis on June 21, 2022, but then 'illegally overstayed in defiance of our laws.'

Twin brothers and soccer players Luis and Carlos Orta Santoro, both 19, were taken into ICE custody on November 5 after being arrested the previous day

Luis and Carlos were region title-winning soccer players for Archer High School in Lawrenceville, Georgia

The brothers were arrested as they returned from visiting their parents, Carlos Enrique Orta and Reyna Santoro de Orta (both left)

The DHS spokesperson told the Daily Mail: 'All their claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and they will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law.'

'To be clear, pending applications do NOT confer legal status,' the statement continued.

Carlos was named the offensive player of the year and Luis the midfield player of the year by their high school this year.

They had received soccer scholarships to attend Wallace State, which they began doing this fall, but now face deportation to Venezuela.

'It's been hell,' Santoro de Orta, their mother, told the outlet.

She added that she supported ICE 'taking away the criminals' but said her children did not fit that description.

A final decision on the brothers' asylum case is still pending as they remain in custody.

The concerned mother claimed police said the twins' car had failed to come to a complete stop at a stop sign.

The brothers were arrested by a Lincoln Police Department officer as they were returning to Wallace State Community College, where they have soccer scholarships

The family applied for asylum protections after legally entering the country on a tourist visa. The DHS said the brothers 'illegally overstayed in defiance of our laws'

The Lincoln Police Department signed a partnership agreement with ICE in July.

ICE said the program allows trained local officers to exercise limited immigration authority during routine police work under federal supervision, according to the Cullman Tribune.

Luis and Carlos were booked into the Talladega County Jail on November 4 and transferred to ICE custody the following day.

Their father, Orta, described how the family was grappling with guilt as they shared what happened to their children.

'If anyone is at fault, it's me. It's us,' Orta told the outlet. 'Because I insist and I will continue to insist that Carlos and Luis came here because of a decision we made.'

He added: 'Carlos and Luis stayed here because of a decision from mom and dad. Carlos and Luis are here because of us.'

The Santoro twins were taken to the Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in southern Louisiana after their arrest, WABE reported.

The brothers have been taken to the the Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in southern Louisiana

The Lincoln Police Department signed an partnership agreement with ICE in July. A department officer arrested the brothers

A friend of the twins, Nicolas Azcarate Florez, said he had spoken to them multiple times since they were taken into custody.

'They've been saying that they've been moved five times, so it has been difficult for them,' Azcarate Florez told the outlet.

Azcarate Florez said the brothers were 'players that you could just give the ball to, and you would know that they would do something good with it.'

'If we needed them, we would know that they would be there to help us out of a sticky situation,' he added.

The brothers were taken into custody on the same week that the Republican Party faced a historic blue wave in the midterm elections that was seen as a rebuke of the GOP's immigration policy.

One of President Donald Trump's first moves afterwards was to name Stephen Miller as the new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Miller, one of Trump's most loyal and longest-serving advisers going back to his first administration, is known for his hardline views on immigration.

Critics have cited Miller as the architect of some of Trump's most divisive policies, including separating migrant families during deportations in the President's first term.

#2156. 'Very insecure' - Emile Heskey reveals Leicester City dressing-room truth about Robbie Savage

Peterborough United appointed Robbie Savage as their new manager on October 2nd, having been impressed by the work he'd done with Forest Green Rovers. His ex-Leicester City teammate, Emile Heskey, has now offered a peak behind the curtain to reveal exactly what the Posh boss is like.

Savage is still juggling his life as a pundit and media personality, alongside the full-time gig with Peterborough in League One.

Naturally, there's been some opposition to that arrangement, and a run of seven games in all competitions without a win heading into this weekend isn't exactly helping his cause.

Ironically, Savage's first game as Peterborough boss came against Leicester on October 10th, with his side racing into a 3-0 lead before seeing the game out to win 3-1, giving the former Fox the ideal start to life in the dugout.

After coming through at Man United and cutting his teeth with Crewe, it had been at Leicester where Savage had made a name for himself in the Premier League.

Heskey has been appearing on the 'Jamie Vardy's Having A Party' podcast, with the two former Leicester strikers trading stories from their time at the club.

In one part, Heskey is quizzed on any 'funny stories' he might have from his time at Filbert Street, where he responds to talk about Savage turning up in a purple Porsche, which Vardy finds easy to believe.

Vardy says: "Stuff like that brings the team together. He’s set himself up, but it’s good for the group."

Heskey totally agrees, saying: "He was really good in taking it (the banter he got)," before revealing to a surprised Vardy: "He actually is quite sensitive and very insecure is Robbie.

"He’s one of those players where, before a game, we’d have to say, ‘We need you, Robbie, come on. You’re the best’.

"He’d be nervous and like he didn’t want to play, pulling out of games. But this is this happy-go-lucky guy that you see all bubbly and that, but he is quite insecure."

Heskey played with Savage at Leicester, before also linking up with him at Birmingham City later in the pair's careers.

FLW looks at who entertains the most, and the least, in League One

As Heskey reveals, Savage was good at taking things on the chin when it came to the banter he got in the changing rooms. He was also pretty good at doing the same thing from rival fans as a player.

Savage finished his Leicester career with 204 appearances for the Foxes, along with 137 at Derby County, 100 at Blackburn Rovers and a further 88 for Birmingham. 346 of his career outings came in the Premier League, and you can tell by the tone of Heskey's voice that he picked up a fair bit of admiration for that.

Moving into coaching isn't easy, but Savage has had stints with Macclesfield and Forest Green, cutting his teeth at the bottom of the game to earn this chance at Peterborough.

It's a slightly different persona he will have to give off as a manager compared to a player, but every inch of his experience will be key to turning things around for Posh.

Their defensive record has been shambolic, and Pochettino needs to fix it as soon as possible. They have conceded 19 goals in the Premier League this season, the third fewest after Crystal Palace and Ipswich Town.

Their defensive struggles could encourage the Old Trafford board to invest in a new centre-back, with Newcastle’s Malick Thiaw emerging as a potential option.

Amid their defensive struggles, Manchester United are among several clubs keeping tabs on Malick Thiaw as they look to address their problems under new manager, Mauricio Pochettino.

Newcastle United have set a massive € 80 million asking price for Malick Thiaw amid growing interest in the German international.

Several top European clubs have the 25-year-old centre-back on their radar after his impressive performances at St James’ Park. However, Newcastle are determined to not lose him on a cheap.

According to reports by Sky Germany, Matthias Jaissle’s side would want at least €80m for Thiaw, who remains under contract with the Magpies until 2029.

The German defender has also earned recognition from national team manager Jurgen Klopp, while Jaissle considers him an important part of his Newcastle side.

Newcastle signed the former Schalke defender from AC Milan in 2025 for a reported €35million.

Since arriving at St James’ Park, Thiaw has established himself as a key figure in the Magpies’ defence, making 64 appearances and contributing five goals and two assists.

His performances have attracted attention from several clubs, but Newcastle are in a strong position given his long-term contract.

Although a departure next summer has not been entirely ruled out, the Magpies are unlikely to entertain any approach that falls short of their €80million valuation.

Manchester United have a clear gap to fill in their defence line. Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez haven’t eased the nerves this season and the Red Devils need a change at the back. Malick Thiaw can be the answer but he isn’t going to be cheap cost United heavy on their pockets.

The big question isn’t the transfer value but whether he is the profile that Mauricio Pochettino needs when he rebuilds Manchester United.

#2154. Pochettino begins Man Utd reign ahead of Liverpool showdown

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Mauricio Pochettino officially begins work as United head coach on Wednesday, just four days before his first match against Liverpool at Anfield.

The 54-year-old replaces Michael Carrick, who was dismissed last week after United won just one of their opening 10 Premier League matches, leaving them 18th in the table.

Pochettino arrives after completing his final assignment with the United States, who beat Haiti 2-0 on Tuesday to secure an 8-0 aggregate victory in their CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final.

The Argentine has signed a contract until the summer of 2029 and is expected to meet his new players and oversee his first training session on Thursday.

Speaking after his final match with the United States, Pochettino acknowledged the challenge awaiting him in Manchester.

“The new challenge is a big challenge, but at the same time it’s adrenaline you want to feel,” he said.

Several members of his coaching staff, including long-time assistant Jesus Perez, travelled to Manchester earlier this week to begin preparations. Pochettino will have limited time to work with his squad before Sunday’s Premier League meeting with Liverpool, which kicks off at 4.30pm GMT.

The former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain manager inherits a United side struggling for results after a difficult opening to the campaign. He previously guided Tottenham to the 2019 Champions League final and won the French league title during his spell with Paris Saint-Germain.

United’s next fixtures also include a Champions League trip to Sporting CP and a home Premier League match against Brentford. Pochettino’s immediate task is to improve United’s league position, beginning with a demanding first match at Anfield.

#2153. Barry Bannan reacts in two words to Jamal Lowe exploits for Sheffield Wednesday v Barnsley

Barry Bannan has issued a two-word reaction to the performance of Sheffield Wednesday teammate, Jamal Lowe, as the Owls made it two league victories in succession under newly-appointed head coach, Dave Challinor.

Having seen off Plymouth Argyle last Saturday, Challinor's first League One outing in charge of Wednesday on the road came in the form of a South Yorkshire derby against Daniel Stendel's lowly Barnsley outfit.

Backed by over 4,800 supporters, Challinor's side didn't disappoint as they raced into a two-goal lead within the first 14 minutes, with Lowe netting his first brace of the campaign.

The Tykes responded five minutes before half-time through the highly-rated Vimal Yonganathan, but back-to-back victories for the first time since September lifted the Owls up to third.

Upon taking the managerial role at Hillsborough, Challinor has plenty of quality and experience at his disposal, with both attributes possessed by Bannan and Lowe in particular.

The latter opened the scoring at Oakwell just eight minutes into the encounter as he side-footed Liam Cooper's knockdown from a free-kick past Cieran Slicker, before doubling the advantage six minutes later as he was found in acres of space by Bannan, then drifting inside and slotting the ball into the bottom-right-hand corner.

Those strikes were the Jamaican's first since his dramatic 98th-minute penalty against Huddersfield Town last month, taking his overall tally up to seven for the season.

Speaking post-match, Lowe claimed that he is capable of taking his tally up to 15 goals, which will be music to the ears of Owls fans, as well as Bannan, who issued a two-word reaction of: "Goals Like", with a picture of him and the versatile figure in celebration.

Across his 93 appearances for the Owls, Lowe has endured a mixed time, even after producing seven goal contributions last term.

In the wins over Plymouth and Barnsley, the 32-year-old has been stationed at left-wing-back, and received praise for his all-round performance from many Wednesdayites.

"Testament to the new manager people say oh J Lowe is lazy can’t run etc and not only does Dave have him run he puts him at LWB where he has to run and gets goals from there on top," said one of those supporters.

Another Wednesday fan commented: "Gave Jamal Lowe stick last couple of weeks but effort for tonight was brilliant. Credit where credits due well done 2 goals along the way! Long may it continue. Honolulu Wednesday!!!"

"Jamal Lowe has turned into peak Roberto Carlos," was a rather humourous summation of his exploits.

Owls fans, how did you view Jamal Lowe's all-round performance against Barnsley? Comment below!

Another verdict read: "Playing Lowe in (his) best position. GOAL. Well done Jamz."

However, not all were overly convinced, with one supporter claiming: "Lowe has no clue how to defend."

Challinor recently went viral due to an image of his notes during the FA Cup defeat to Oldham Athletic in his first game in charge, and despite a youthful side being defeated heavily in the EFL Trophy to Accrington Stanley, his league ventures have started strongly.

Wednesday are still not flawless, but the outlook of their season is certainly more rosey than in the final weeks of Henrik Pedersen's tenure, as they can only drop to fifth depending on Saturday's results.

FLW have ranked the 10 best EFL League One stadiums so far in the 2026/27 season, including Bradford City and Sheffield Wednesday.

With Plymouth expected to challenge for promotion, last weekend's 3-0 success was seen as a statement, whilst different characteristics earned three points against their local rivals.

Challinor will now hope his side benefit from an extra day's recovery for when they travel to Stevenage on Tuesday.

#2152. ‘Sometimes to love is to let go’, former Man Utd midfielder announces retirement

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Former Manchester United midfielder Juan Mata has announced his retirement from professional football at the age of 38, bringing an end to a beautiful career of around 20 years.

The Spaniard went on to win one of the biggest trophies in professional football. The former Manchester United midfielder confirmed his decision on Wednesday after ending his playing career with Australian side Melbourne Victory.

Mata enjoyed a memorable spell at Manchester United after arriving from Chelsea in January 2014. He spent more than eight years at Old Trafford, making 285 appearances, scoring 51 goals and winning four trophies.

His first trophy with Manchester United came in the 2016 FA Cup final against Crystal Palace. He also helped the club win the Community Shield, League Cup and Europa League during the 2016/17 campaign.

Before moving to Manchester, Juan Mata had established himself as one of Chelsea’s most creative players. He won the club’s Player of the Year award in both of his first two full seasons at Stamford Bridge before eventually joining United as David Moyes’ marquee signing.

Mata probably had the biggest moments of his career in the Spain shirt. He earned 41 international caps and scored 10 goals, becoming part of the most talented Spanish team in history. He went on to win the 2010 FIFA World Cup and Euro 2012 with Spain while etching his name in Spanish football history with a goal in Spain’s 4-0 victory over Italy in the European Championship final.

After leaving Manchester United in 2022, the midfielder continued his career with Galatasaray, Vissel Kobe and Western Sydney Wanderers before joining Melbourne Victory in September 2025.

His final season in Australia was an impressive one. Mata registered five goals and 13 assists, won the Johnny Warren Medal and earned a place in the A-League Team of the Season.

Sometimes, to love… is to let go. THANKS FOOTBALL. ⚽️❤️♾️A veces, amar… es dejar ir. GRACIAS FÚTBOL. ⚽️❤️♾️ pic.twitter.com/v7otd6AyOq

Reflecting on his decision, Mata spoke about the reason that kept him playing for so many years.

“I was able to keep going for so many years because of the sheer joy of playing,” he said.

He also made it clear that retirement would not mean walking away from football altogether.

“Football will never leave my life. There are so many ways to continue loving the game.”

Manchester United also paid tribute to their former midfielder, writing on social media: “Great player, better person. Thank you for representing our colours with class, Juan.”

Great player, better person.Thank you for representing our colours with class, Juan ❤️

Mata leaves the game on his own terms and more importantly as a winner. With all the trophies he won, United will remember him for a lot more. The persona he had, the brilliant assists, goals like that one on Anfield and more importantly the joy he brough to United fans in a difficult time at the club.

#2151. On The Road: Overpowered by County, but Accies are making small steps in the long road back from the abyss

Published: 08:28 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 10:25 EST, 15 November 2026

The depth of the descent of Hamilton Accies and Ross County would make it understandable if tickets for a fixture between the two carried warning about the bends when leaving New Douglas Park.

The decompression sickness caused by emerging from a League One fixture for two sides who should be much higher must be severe. There may, however, be a positive prognosis.

Accies, despite their defeat, are whispering about stability, even though ‘legacy debt’ has to be faced, perhaps contested.

County, meanwhile, will not say it even in a whisper but Saturday’s victory takes them eight points clear at the top and heavily fancied for the title. The Staggies have one set of hooves in the Championship.

Scottish football, of course, does not restrict itself to the cliched fare of top of the table clashes so New Douglas Park hosted a striker who is 39 later this month, a winger who was once a Scottish international, and a gentleman in the stands who once played against George Best. And a Ross County fan who regularly travels up from North Wales.

These exotic avenues demand to be explored but perennial questions about the financial health of the Accies had to be asked, too, after reports this week stating that hospitality packages at the club were being suspended.

An Accies fan feels the pain of defeat during Saturday's home loss to Ross County

Allan Currie, chairman, answered them over a half-time pie.

‘We have come on in leaps and bounds but every week seems to throw up different challenges,’ he said. ‘We have a level of debt that we have inherited and we are working with the creditors to try to navigate our way through that.’

Matters on the field are positive, despite Saturday’s defeat.

‘The guys on the pitch, manager, and his staff have been unbelievable. Surviving in this league last season was phenomenal given what they were going through but it couldn’t be better now,’ he said. ‘Off the pitch, we are fighting with the different challenges we have. We are in a much better place even if we are not out the woods yet.’

Asked what the level of pressure on him, he said: ‘I am the guy on the ground but Rob Edwards is carrying out negotiations.’

Edwards, through his Morley Group, took over the club earlier this year but has been sideswiped by a number of claims for payment. However, Currie has faith in the owner.

‘Without him, the club would not survive. Rob should take all the credit,’ he said.

Asked what the short-term aims for the club were, Currie replied with a smile: ‘A goal in the second half would be good.’ A goal was scored but not for the Accies.

But the club remain in second place and the play-offs seem a more than reasonable prospect.

Ross County goalscorer Kieran Phillips battles with Hamilton's Kai Smutek

With 10 minutes to go, Hamilton brought on their latest signing. Barrie McKay, who has played for Scotland and scored for Rangers in a Scottish Cup semi-final against Celtic. His considerable achievements, though, paled in comparison to the subject of a casual conversation in the bar before the match.

‘I played against George Best,’ said Alan McDougall, with an air so off-hand one could have believed he was merely ordering another pint.

‘Yes, I played 200 games for the Accies. Davie McParland brought me here as a 21-year-old and I played for about six years. I went to Stranraer for a year and then went down south. I played against Best with the Accies.’

The Northern Irish genius played for Hibernian in 1979-80. ‘He was well past his best and that was sad,’ said McDougall. Best’s addiction to alcohol had taken a severe toll.

‘I came back to watch games five or six years ago,’ said McDougall. ‘When the club went to Clyde, it destroyed me. What is fantastic is that the people that are now in control seem to be turning it around.’

There was a mood of cautious optimism from other fans. ‘I have been a fan since forever, well the 1980s at least,’ said Gavin Fullarton. ‘I have seen this team in every division. I have seen them in the downs and downs. But I think we are going in the right direction. So far.’

He added: ‘The new guys seem to know what they are doing. They are communicative.’

There were 1,216 fans in the ground on Saturday with 300 stalwarts travelling down from the north. Colin Richardson, an Accies supporter, was asked why so many had stuck by the club.

‘It’s about loyalty,’ he said. ‘You can’t pick and choose when you support your team. At the moment it is all about small steps. It has to be about stability.’

A Ross County fan had travelled up from North Wales. The journey to Scotland is a familiar one for Ian Ellson. ‘I have been all over Scotland to watch Ross County,’ he said. ‘Twenty years ago I visited Ross County and I was spoiled rotten. I decided to follow them.’

A social worker, he averages one visit a month. ‘I live and breathe Ross County,’ he said. ‘This season we are going up.’

Welsh Staggies fan Ian Elson and Englishman Ray Griffiths travelled far for Saturday's game

Brian Graham would not be so bullish. He is 39 this month and has learned enough about football to know that predictions are made only to make the speaker seem foolish down the line.

He was, though, expansive about what is happening at County. He joined the club for the second time in the summer after Stuart Kettlewell, the manager, convinced him of the ambitions in Dingwall.

‘This is a club where I have had success before so I know how good a club it can be,’ he said. ‘It’s not been great for a couple of seasons but in the summer the manager set out his stall very early. It was about leaving egos at the door, building a togetherness and having a change of culture at the club. I think you are seeing that now.’

The early signs were good for the striker who dropped down from Falkirk in the Premiership to play in Dingwall.

‘We had good pre-season performances against Aberdeen and Dundee and that was a solid building block,’ he said.

Brian Graham celebrates after scoring his 21st goal of the season for County

Graham converted a first-half penalty to reach a tally of 21 goals this season and the Christmas trees are not up yet. ‘I get a lot of plaudits for scoring goals but others in the team are scoring a lot too,’ he said. ‘We are scoring team goals.’

Has he set a target for the season? ‘When I came back I knew I had to score 13 to reach 50 goals for the club in two spells,’ he said. ‘I always set down targets in a wee black book but now I might need to readjust that.’

It was a night of adjustment for Darian MacKinnon. He had set a victory target but was condemned to accept defeat. He would not concede the league race was over. ‘We have to play them twice,’ he said.

He added ‘We are going in the right direction. The owners have put money in and they have backed us.’

Asked to pinpoint a factor that has contributed to the team sitting second, he said: ‘The most positive thing for me this season is that this is now a good place to come into your work after the last three or four seasons. We are all actually enjoying coming to our work.’

There is work to be done on and off the pitch but the Accies are surviving. And that is the biggest result.

Manchester United could make an ambitious move for former Liverpool sporting director Michael Edwards, with the Glazer family reportedly keen to bring the highly rated executive to Old Trafford.

According to a report from popular Indykaila News on X, the Glazer side of United’s ownership wants Michael Edwards to take full control of the club’s football operations.

Exclusive: Manchester United board member eyes extraordinary move for Michael EdwardsA Manchester United board member is pushing for the appointment of former Liverpool director of football Michael Edwards. A major U-turn from Edwards would be needed to join the #MUFC project.…

With the Glazers interested in the appointment, such a move would be a major shift from the current arrangement at Old Trafford, where Sir Jim Ratcliffe and INEOS are currently responsible for overseeing the football department.

Edwards is regarded as one of the most influential executives in modern English football, having played a major role in building Liverpool’s squad under Jurgen Klopp.

Michael Edwards joined Liverpool in 2011 before being appointed as their sporting director in November 2016. He oversaw player recruitment bring in some of the biggest names at Liverpool including Mo Salah and Sadio Mane. Liverpool saw one of their most successful years in modern history in the Premier League and Europe under Jurgen Klopp while Edwards oversaw the footballing operations.

Manchester United have previously attempted to bring Edwards to Old Trafford before, but were unsuccessful.

Following his departure from Liverpool in 2022, Edwards turned down approaches from several clubs, including Manchester United and Chelsea. He then returned to Fenway Sports Group in March 2024 to oversee FSG’s wider football operations.

His second spell with FSG came to an end in July 2026. That exit has reopened the door for many interested clubs including Manchester United. However, there is no confirmation that Edwards is considering another move to United.

#2149. What Dave Challinor said after Sheffield Wednesday win has sparked a reaction

The new Sheffield Wednesday manager had qualified praise for his team's performance following his team's South Yorkshire derby win at Barnsley.

Following a slightly rocky start, Dave Challinor is starting to settle in as the new manager of Sheffield Wednesday. Two Jamal Lowe goals in the opening stages of their Friday night trip to Barnsley gave them the perfect start at Oakwell, but Wednesday were pegged back by a goal from Vimal Yoganathan and ended up hanging on a little for the win.

The three points lifted them to third place in the table, though as this was a Friday night fixture, they might well not still be there by the end of the weekend, and after the match Challinor had some praise for his team's performance, though he was very clear that they still have a lot of work to do to get the team to the level of the manager's satisfaction.

Speaking to the Sheffield Wednesday media team after his team's win at Barnsley as posted to the social media platfiorm X, Challinor was qualified in praise of his team's performance: "I'm really pleased with the win. I won't say I'm disappointed with our performance, but I think there's loads more to come from us. As I've just said to the players, my job's not to really over-celebrate wins, it's to look at things analytically and make sure we're better, and there's stacks more to come from us."

And it's clear that Challinor wants to see his team playing on the front foot more: "Scoring two goals is the best thing that could happen and probably the worst thing too because, from a player's perspective, we became really passive, too negative, and almost thought the game was won. We have and will continue to take ourselves out of our comfort zone and expose ourselves a little bit. We need to defend miles higher up."

What tweaks would you want made to the Sheffield Wednesday team during the January transfer window? Let us know in the comments below!

Asked about the performance of Jamal Lowe, Challinor revealed that the forward was disappointed not to receive the Man of the Match Award, given his two goals: "It's nice to score from a set-piece again. Jamal's done another brilliant job for the team in a position that's not his position, but he's got two goals from there, which is great for him, and on another day he gets himself a hat-trick, potentially. Strangely, he hasn't got the Match of the Match from Sky, which he's disappointed about, but we can deal with that because we've got three points."

And he also singled out Liam Cooper for praise: "Coops is a leader for us. With him, his experience and his age, he is going to be important, but as I've told him, I've got to get him to get the rest of them up the pitch and not be defending too deep. I've been there. The last thing you want to be is a centre-half who's not rapid against strikers who want to run in behind, looking behind and having loads of space between your backside and your own goal. But it's going to paramount to what we do and how we go about it. And for him to get through two 90 minutes in the last week is brilliant for us. We've got to recover and make sure we're good to go on Tuesday."

The Owls striker's performance was key in Friday's local derby win at Oakwell
